title: Evaluation, Drift Detection & Automated Pipelines
desc: Build a golden-set eval harness, detect input and output drift statistically, and wire both into a nightly pipeline that pages you before users notice a regression.
content:
Shipping the Model Is the Easy Part

A model that passed your smoke tests on day one can quietly degrade by week four — the underlying weights haven't changed, but the traffic hitting it has. A prompt template a product team tweaked upstream, a new user segment with different phrasing, a provider-side model swap behind an API you don't control. Without an evaluation and drift pipeline running continuously, the first signal you get is a support ticket.

🔑
What this lesson builds
A golden-set eval harness you can run on every deploy, a statistical drift detector you can run nightly against live traffic, and an orchestration script that ties both together and pages you when either one crosses a threshold.

Offline Evaluation: Golden Sets, Metrics, and Judges

Before you can detect a regression, you need a fixed, versioned reference: a golden dataset of prompts paired with expected behavior (an exact answer, a rubric, or a "chosen vs rejected" pair). Golden sets should be curated from real production failures as much as from synthetic cases — every incident postmortem should end with a new row added to the set.

MethodGood forWeakness
Exact match / regexStructured outputs, classification, tool-call argumentsUseless for open-ended generation
ROUGE / BLEUSummarization, translation, cheap regression signalPoor correlation with human judgment on chat-style output
LLM-as-judgeOpen-ended quality, tone, faithfulness, helpfulnessJudge bias (position, verbosity, self-preference) — needs calibration against humans
Human evalGround truth for calibrating automated judgesSlow, expensive — sample, don't scale
📄
LLM-as-judge is a calibrated instrument, not ground truth
Zheng et al. (2023) found GPT-4 judges agree with human preference over 80% of the time on MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena, but flagged systematic biases — judges favor longer answers (verbosity bias) and the first answer shown (position bias). Randomize answer order and periodically spot-check the judge against a small human-labeled sample before trusting it for regression gating.

A Runnable Eval Harness

This harness loads a golden set, calls your served model (the vLLM OpenAI-compatible endpoint from Day 3), scores each response with an LLM judge, and prints a pass-rate report you can gate a deploy on.

Python · eval_harness.py
import json
from dataclasses import dataclass
from openai import OpenAI

candidate = OpenAI(base_url="http://:8000/v1", api_key="not-needed")
judge     = OpenAI(api_key="sk-...")  # a strong external judge model, kept separate from the candidate

@dataclass
class GoldenCase:
    prompt: str
    rubric: str  # what a correct answer must contain / avoid

def load_golden_set(path: str) -> list[GoldenCase]:
    rows = json.load(open(path))
    return [GoldenCase(**row) for row in rows]

def judge_response(prompt: str, rubric: str, response: str) -> bool:
    verdict = judge.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o",
        messages=[{
            "role": "user",
            "content": (
                f"Prompt: {prompt}\nRubric: {rubric}\nResponse: {response}\n\n"
                "Does the response satisfy the rubric? Reply with exactly PASS or FAIL."
            ),
        }],
        temperature=0.0,
    )
    return "PASS" in verdict.choices[0].message.content.upper()

def run_eval(golden_path: str) -> dict:
    cases = load_golden_set(golden_path)
    passed = 0
    failures = []
    for case in cases:
        resp = candidate.chat.completions.create(
            model="meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct",
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": case.prompt}],
            temperature=0.1,
        ).choices[0].message.content
        ok = judge_response(case.prompt, case.rubric, resp)
        passed += int(ok)
        if not ok:
            failures.append({"prompt": case.prompt, "response": resp})
    pass_rate = passed / len(cases)
    return {"pass_rate": pass_rate, "total": len(cases), "failures": failures}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    report = run_eval("golden_set.json")
    print(f"Pass rate: {report['pass_rate']:.1%} ({report['total']} cases)")
    if report["failures"]:
        print(f"{len(report['failures'])} failures — see failures.json")
        json.dump(report["failures"], open("failures.json", "w"), indent=2)

Production Drift: Three Different Failure Modes

  • Input drift — the distribution of incoming prompts shifts (new user segment, new feature sending different traffic). The model itself is unchanged, but it's now facing out-of-distribution inputs.
  • Output / behavioral drift — for the same kind of input, the distribution of outputs changes (a provider silently updates a model behind an API, a routing change picks a different backend, sampling parameters changed).
  • Concept drift — the relationship between input and "correct" output changes in the real world (a policy changed, a product feature was deprecated) even though nothing in your stack moved.
Population Stability Index (PSI)
PSI = Σᵢ (aᵢ − bᵢ) × ln(aᵢ / bᵢ)

Where aᵢ is the proportion of the baseline population in bin i, and bᵢ is the proportion of the current population in the same bin. Bin either raw features (prompt length, token-level n-gram frequency) or, more robustly, embedding-space clusters. PSI < 0.1 is stable, 0.1–0.25 is worth watching, > 0.25 typically means the distribution has shifted enough to matter.

Python · psi_drift.py — embedding-space PSI
import numpy as np

def psi(baseline: np.ndarray, current: np.ndarray, bins: int = 10) -> float:
    """baseline / current: 1-D arrays, e.g. PCA-reduced embedding scores"""
    edges = np.quantile(baseline, np.linspace(0, 1, bins + 1))
    edges[0], edges[-1] = -np.inf, np.inf

    base_counts, _ = np.histogram(baseline, bins=edges)
    curr_counts, _ = np.histogram(current, bins=edges)

    a = base_counts / base_counts.sum()
    b = curr_counts / curr_counts.sum()
    # avoid log(0) / div-by-0 on empty bins
    a = np.clip(a, 1e-6, None)
    b = np.clip(b, 1e-6, None)
    return float(np.sum((a - b) * np.log(a / b)))

# baseline: embed a fixed window of last month's prompts (e.g. via a small sentence-transformer),
# project to 1-D with PCA for a cheap univariate PSI, or run PSI per-dimension and take the max.
drift_score = psi(baseline_scores, current_window_scores)
print(f"PSI: {drift_score:.3f}")
A nightly job samples production traffic, scores it against the golden set, computes drift against a rolling baseline, and pages on-call only when a threshold is crossed.

Wiring It Into an Automated Pipeline

You don't need Airflow to get 90% of the value. A single scheduled script that samples traffic, runs both checks, and posts to a webhook is enough to start — you can graduate to a real orchestrator once the checks themselves are trustworthy.

Python · nightly_pipeline.py
import json, requests, schedule, time
from eval_harness import run_eval
from psi_drift import psi
from embeddings import embed_prompts  # your own thin wrapper around a sentence-transformer

SLACK_WEBHOOK = "https://hooks.slack.com/services/..."
PASS_RATE_FLOOR = 0.90
PSI_CEILING = 0.25

def alert(message: str) -> None:
    requests.post(SLACK_WEBHOOK, json={"text": message})

def nightly_job() -> None:
    # 1. eval against golden set
    report = run_eval("golden_set.json")
    if report["pass_rate"] < PASS_RATE_FLOOR:
        alert(f":rotating_light: Eval pass rate dropped to {report['pass_rate']:.1%} "
              f"(floor {PASS_RATE_FLOOR:.0%}) — {len(report['failures'])} failing cases")

    # 2. drift against yesterday's sampled traffic vs a 30-day rolling baseline
    baseline = json.load(open("baseline_embeddings.json"))
    todays_prompts = json.load(open("sampled_traffic.json"))
    current = embed_prompts(todays_prompts)
    drift_score = psi(baseline, current)
    if drift_score > PSI_CEILING:
        alert(f":chart_with_upwards_trend: Input drift PSI={drift_score:.3f} "
              f"exceeds ceiling {PSI_CEILING} — review sampled_traffic.json")

    print(f"[{time.strftime('%Y-%m-%d %H:%M')}] pass_rate={report['pass_rate']:.1%} psi={drift_score:.3f}")

schedule.every().day.at("02:00").do(nightly_job)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    while True:
        schedule.run_pending()
        time.sleep(60)
💡
Run this as a systemd timer, not a while-loop
The schedule long-running loop above is fine for a prototype, but in production prefer a systemd timer (or cron) calling python nightly_job.py directly — same pattern you used for the vLLM service in Day 3. A crashed while-loop silently stops paging; a systemd timer that fails to fire shows up in systemctl list-timers.

What to Monitor and When to Page

SignalCadenceSuggested alert threshold
Eval pass-rate (golden set)Every deploy + nightly< 90% of last-known-good baseline
Input drift (PSI on prompt embeddings)Nightly, rolling 30-day baselinePSI > 0.25
p95 request latency / TTFTReal-time (from Day 6's metrics)> 2× the Day 1 capacity-planning target
Error rate (5xx, timeouts)Real-time> 1% over 5 min window
Token usage / cost per requestDaily rollup> 20% week-over-week increase
🧠 Check your understanding
Q1. Your golden-set pass rate is unchanged, but PSI on prompt embeddings has jumped from 0.05 to 0.4 over a week. What does this most likely indicate?
Q2. Why keep the judge model in eval_harness.py separate from the candidate model being evaluated?
Q3. In the PSI formula, what does a bin with a large baseline proportion but zero current-window observations do to the score if left unclipped?
